Our thoughts are with the children and families who have lost loved ones, homes, and livelihoods. UNICEF is on the ground, and we are doing everything we can to help them recover. Globally, humanitarian and development needs for children continue to grow, even as the resources available to meet them shrink. Meanwhile, rapid technological change is transforming childhood itself, bringing extraordinary opportunities, but also risks that the world must address. The focus of this year's General Assembly is particularly relevant, the United Nations that delivers for all. For UNICEF, this means the United Nations that does everything it can to improve the lives of children. Excellencies, as you know well, the UN is in the midst of transformation and UNICEF is fully engaged in that UNAD process. We see real opportunities to make the United Nations more effective, more coherent, and better equipped for the challenges of the world today. UNICEF brings broad experience, our operational footprint, and the tremendous talent of our people to that effort. At the global level, UNICEF, WFP, and UNDOS are co-leading work on integrated supply chains. New approaches piloted in Afghanistan, Gaza, Haiti, Somalia, and Sudan are already demonstrating savings in transport and logistics costs. UNICEF is also co-leading work on the UN Data Commons, which will bring together official data from 28 UN entities to give governments a clearer picture of who's being left behind and where action is needed most. For UNICEF, UN reform is not an abstract exercise. Its success will be judged by whether children are safer, healthier, better educated, and better able to realize their rights. We are fully committed to this effort. Excellencies, in 1946, in the aftermath of the Second World War, millions of children were hungry, displaced, and facing an uncertain future. In response, the international community made a remarkable choice. Countries divided by war agreed that a peaceful, prosperous future depended on investing in children. That choice gave birth to UNICEF. And in December of this year, we will mark UNICEF's 80th anniversary. What began as an emergency fund for children became something more significant, a global commitment to the idea that every child has rights and that societies are stronger when they invest in children. Over eight decades, UNICEF has helped drive a revolution in child survival, working with governments and partners to bring simple, proven interventions within reach for millions of families and saving countless lives in the process. Vaccines have protected generations of children from diseases that once routinely killed or disabled millions. Oral rehydration therapy transformed the treatment of childhood diarrhea. Support for breastfeeding, better nutrition, clean water and sanitation, and stronger primary health care have given millions more children the chance not only to survive their earliest years, but to grow and to thrive. Together, these efforts have contributed to one of the great achievements of our time. Since 1990, the global under five mortality rate has fallen by 60%. Excuse me. Behind that figure are millions of children who not only survived, but are healthy and educated. Diseases that once threatened children around the world have been pushed back dramatically. Polio, for example, has been eradicated in all but a few places, bringing the world closer than ever to ending that horrible disease. UNICEF also helped champion a different understanding of childhood itself. Children not simply as people in need, but as individuals with rights. The adoption of the Convention on the Rights of the Child in 1989 established the most widely ratified human rights treaty in history. Since then, UNICEF has worked with governments to translate those rights into laws, policies, and services, from birth registration and education to protection from violence, harmful practices, and the grave violations children face in war. Excuse me. Throughout those 80 years, humanitarian action has remained a critical part of UNICEF's DNA. From the children displaced by war in Europe who inspired UNICEF's creation to children affected by conflict and disasters today, UNICEF has always been there, often in some of the world's most difficult places. None of this progress belongs to UNICEF alone. It belongs to governments that invested in children and in the systems that support them. to health workers, teachers, social workers, to communities and civil society, to our United Nations partners, to donors, businesses, our UNICEF national committees, and millions of individual supporters, and of course to children and young people themselves. Our experience provides an important lesson for all of us that humanitarian action is indispensable, but so too is the sustained and very hard work of development, strengthening health and education systems, expanding access to water and sanitation, improving nutrition and social protection, and helping governments invest in their youngest citizens. For 80 years, UNICEF has accompanied countries on that development journey. Excellencies, children today face challenges and opportunities that the founders of UNICEF could only have imagined. Perhaps nowhere is this clearer than in the areas of digital technology and artificial intelligence. AI has extraordinary potential for children, widening access to knowledge, helping children with disabilities, supporting learning, and bringing information and services to communities historically left behind. But opportunities without safeguards can deepen inequality and cause harm. We have a responsibility to shape those systems now. We cannot repeat the mistakes made with social media, responding to harms only after they have become deeply embedded. Safeguarding children from online sexual abuse is a critical piece of this work. So too is protecting children's data, ensuring that AI in schools, health systems and other services advances children's development and giving children a voice in decisions about technologies that shape their future. UNICEF is helping to move this agenda forward. Earlier this year, we worked with the G7 to establish the first common principles addressing children in the digital environment. And in July, UNICEF brought a child's child rights perspective to the first global dialogue on AI governance in Geneva, advocating for children's rights and safety to be built into AI governance and for children themselves to have a voice in shaping it. Mr. President, I want to recognize your leadership in helping to convene that important dialogue. Beyond AI, the development agenda faces other significant challenges. Today, excuse me, 273 million children and young people are out of school. while hundreds of millions more are in school but not acquiring the foundational skills they need. We must urgently tackle this learning crisis and ensure that technology strengthens rather than substitutes for investment in teachers and education systems. We must also accelerate progress on safe water and sanitation. Today, 2.1 billion people still lack safe drinking water. while 3.4 billion lack adequate sanitation, which puts them at risk of terrible diseases like cholera. The UN Water Conference this December is an important opportunity to accelerate action on these services, which are fundamental to children's health, dignity, and development. In addition, we must confront the scourge of violence against children. More than half of the world's children experience some form of violence every year. in their homes, schools, communities, and increasingly online. The consequences can follow children throughout their lives. At the same time, environmental threats from extreme heat and air pollution to contaminated water and toxic substances are having a growing impact on children's health and development. These challenges vary, but the lesson of the last 80 years applies to all of them. Lasting progress comes from strong partnership and sustained investment in the systems that children depend on. Excellencies, for some children, the threats they face every day are immediate and life-threatening. In the Democratic Republic of the Congo, children are confronting the country's worst Ebola outbreak on record. More than 300 children have died, and the impact of the deadly disease goes far beyond the immediate physical consequences. In the outbreak's hotspots, use of essential health services fell by more than 40% between April and June. Routine childhood vaccinations have sharply declined, while maternal health care and other essential services have also been disrupted. UNICEF is working with the government, WHO, Africa CDC, and other partners to contain the outbreak and to keep health facilities safe and functioning, maintaining the services children and families depend on. Our teams are also responding to immense humanitarian needs in the state of Palestine and across the Middle East, in Darfur and elsewhere in Sudan, in Myanmar, Nepal, Ukraine, Yemen, and in other crises around the world. UNICEF is providing the emergency health, nutrition, water and sanitation, education, and protection support. This work is made possible through the incredible dedication and sacrifice made by UNICEF staff on the ground in these challenging environments. Keeping in mind the lessons of the past 80 years, we must look beyond immediate response to what comes next. We must respond to crises while planting the seeds for future recovery and development. In Syria and Venezuela, UNICEF is supporting children and communities as they recover and rebuild. And in Lebanon and Gaza, recovery and reconstruction will be essential to restoring the basic services and systems children desperately need. If we get these transitions right, they can become opportunities for hope to rebuild not simply what existed before, but stronger, more resilient systems for children. However, in many places, our humanitarian action faces fundamental constraints. We cannot reach children when access is denied. We cannot sustain lifesaving services without adequate resources. And humanitarian action requires respect by all parties for their obligations under international law. Children and civilian infrastructure must be protected. Humanitarian workers must be able to reach children safely. And parties to conflict must uphold their obligations under international law. Excellencies, our ability to deliver in both humanitarian and development settings is being tested by an increasingly difficult funding environment. Core resources from our public sector partners fell by 31% between 2024 and 2025 alone, reaching the lowest level in UNICEF's history. This matters because core resources are the foundation on which much of UNICEF's work is built. Core resources sustain the expertise and country presence that allow us to help governments strengthen systems, manage risks, and deliver results. They give us the flexibility to allocate resources where the potential impact for children is greatest and to leverage additional resources and partnerships. I'm also pleased to report that private sector core resources are outperforming expectations. To our national committees whose fundraising and advocacy help drive that extraordinary support, a huge, huge thank you. And thank you as well to all of our partners who give UNICEF the trust and flexibility to direct resources where they can achieve the greatest results for children. We will consider both the structured funding dialogue and our updated financial estimates during this board session. I hope those discussions reaffirm a simple principle, ambition for children must be matched by the quality as well as the quantity of resources because cutting investment in children does not make their needs disappear. It merely shifts the cost into the future, into weaker health and education systems, greater inequality, instability, and lost human potential. Excellencies, 80 years ago, the world stood at a crossroads. leaders emerging from devastating conflict made a choice that the lives and futures of children were worth protecting. We have seen the dividends of that commitment. We stand at another crossroads today. The fundamental question is remarkably similar. What kind of future will we choose? Will we allow decades of progress for children to stall, or will we invest in the systems that make it possible for children to survive and thrive? Will technology deepen inequality and expose children to new harms? Or will it shape around their rights and their safety and potential? UNICEF's 80th anniversary is not simply a moment to look back. It is a responsibility to look forward. The future is not something that simply happens to us. It's built decision by decision, investment by investment, partnership by partnership. Our responsibility is to choose wisely, to choose children, to choose investment in their futures, and to support a United Nations that delivers for every child. Thank you very much.

Distinguished delegates, as UNICEF enters its ninth decade, challenges facing children are becoming more complex, but are fundamental.

Mr. President, Madam Executive Director, we are grateful to UNICEF for its tireless work for Ukrainian children amid Russia's continuing war of aggression. This work is more important than ever. That very same day, hundreds of kilometers away, Three more were killed in the Makayev region. Russia attacked Kiev today, this very day, with ballistic missiles overnight and launched another drone attack in the morning just as children were preparing to go to school. Thank you, Mr. President. Allow me to thank you, the Bureau and all members of the Executive Board for your leadership. Bulgaria remains committed to engaging constructively throughout this session. Thank you, distinguished representative of Bulgaria. Before we proceed, I kindly ask Edie Russell to respond to some of the remarks and comments heard so far. Please, you have the floor.

Great, thank you so much. And again, thank you so much, all of you, for the really thoughtful comments. Very much appreciate them, and will do my best here to respond. To the colleague from China, just two things. One, you know, I am... And I know we expressed this publicly, but very sorry about the challenges that China and Nepal are facing in the mudslides. I know how horrific that is and very much want to extend our condolences and concern for the people who are affected by that. And I understand the joint search and rescue is underway, but I know how difficult those situations are. So first, let me say that. Second, I do want to Thank you for the comments about the CPDs. You know, from our perspective, the country program documents are so important because they do reflect the priorities of the country, and we negotiate those carefully. We agree to exactly what we are trying to achieve and what the measurements will be, and so I appreciate the support for that. So the colleague from Sweden. a couple of things. Appreciate the comments on the importance of core resources. Many of you have expressed that. Just to say, I just want to be clear about this. About 80 percent of our core resources go directly to programs. And the key, and Kitty will say this, I'm sure, because she says it all the time, and she's so right, that core is an important part of the overall ecosystem, the funding ecosystem, that includes pooled resources, it includes money that is allocated for certain purposes, but core is a critical part of that overall composition. And I think, you know, the recognition for that is absolutely so important and very, I think, central to our ability. If we don't have the core resources, it so reduces our ability to do what we need to do in the world. And so just a huge thank you to you for that. I would say on the, you raised the point also on visibility. And I think again, Kitty may come back to this when she does her presentation, but we very much wanna recognize and demonstrate the results that we see for the contributions that your governments are making. And visibility is an important part of what we're working on. Many of you know Mandeep who runs our I don't know, we keep changing the names of our divisions, but I call it PPD, but I think it has a new name now, PP, I don't know what the heck it is, but anyway, the point is she works with the governments, and I think we're really focused on visibility and trying to make sure that your governments get the visibility they need for the contributions they make, and very much appreciate that. To the colleague from Slovenia, thank you for mentioning this point about the complexity of emergencies. I think, you know, Others have said it as well, but I do think trying to operate in those environments, as you can imagine, is not just difficult, right? It is difficult, but it is also dangerous for our teams. And I think you also mentioned the importance of UNICEF staff, as have others. It starts to become a cliche, but the truth is we could never do any of the work we do without our staff. Staff at UNICEF is incredibly committed. It's one of the reasons why the work we did last year, what we call FFI, but sort of cutting our staff and moving people to different duty stations and all the rest of it was so painful because people come to UNICEF because they want to help children. That's very much a part of their DNA. And I think, you know, they take extraordinary risks. They put their their own needs and the needs of their family sometimes behind those of the children they're trying to serve. And I really appreciate the fact that you all recognize that and understand how difficult that is. Again, how hard it was for us to let any of those people go from UNICEF, it was really painful. And I just very much appreciate the board's acknowledgement of that. To the colleague from Korea, I think I always love the Korea story. So thank you for mentioning that at the beginning, because I think when you look at Korea and see how far the country has come and how grateful the people of Korea are for the help that they received and how much they in turn want to help others, I find that story to be really Just very encouraging and we're always grateful to hear it, but very much appreciate your comments about that. Also, thank you for mentioning the IFIs. You know, I haven't mentioned them yet. Again, Kitty probably will come back to that at some point, but IFIs, the regional development banks, the World Bank, absolutely critical partners to UNICEF. We are, we work a lot with them and continue to look for opportunities to try to, not just do projects or work together, but also to make sure that our missions are aligned. And to the colleague from Turkey, again, very important comments. One, you mentioned child protection. I did want to come back on that for one point, which is to say that, you know, we estimate that one in six adolescent girls around the world faces some form of partner violence. And protecting children, protecting adolescents in those spaces is absolutely critical because those are terrible things that happen to young people. Trying to make sure the protection services are in shape to the extent that we can, that there are social workers and others who can try to be helpful in this space, trying to develop those systems in countries is really critical for our work. And I very much appreciate that comment. To the colleague from Norway, you made many important points, but one thing I wanted to highlight, which is you mentioned education in emergencies. And UNICEF, when you look at the constellation of challenges children are facing in emergencies, basic survival, you know, food, shelter, some kind of health care, sometimes education gets short shrift in that. And our view and our position is that education is life saving. We've got to make sure that children in these emergencies are able to access education. We see many of these emergencies extend for long periods of time, and to imagine children out of school for all that time is really painful. So thank you so much for mentioning that. To the colleague from Nigeria, first of all, I had a fantastic visit to Nigeria, so huge thank you for that. I really, I got to see a lot of what you're describing and really very much appreciated that. I do think that the the point you made about the digital environment, we keep coming back to that because, first of all, it's very much on everyone's mind, I think, because of all the conversation about AI, but really thinking about, yes, there are tremendous opportunities for children in this space, and we are engaged in a lot of these conversations about how we can use AI to help support and train teachers, how we can use AI, Omar does a lot of this work, how can we use AI to support healthcare workers. And we see that, and we see enormous potential for that, but we also are very mindful of the dangers for children in that environment. And, you know, sometimes these children are sitting, they're just right at these screens, and controlling what they see there and what sort of impact they have on them is really critical. And I think we've really got to keep a very balanced approach to that issue. To the colleague from Guatemala, again made some very important points. One point I want to come back on climate. You know, we did a report maybe two years ago now estimating that a billion children live in, I think, 33 different countries that are at very extremely high risk of different climate challenges. It could be high heat. air pollution, cyclones, flooding, all of the rest of it. And, you know, we're really thinking about how we can help these children live in communities that are more resilient and able to respond or prevent some of these challenges because children are incredibly vulnerable to them. To the colleague from Ukraine, did want to mention sort of a broader point. Thank you for your comments. And I did see the schools that you referred to underground when I visited. But, you know, we estimate that one in six children in the world lives in a conflict zone or is fleeing from a conflict zone. And imagine how disruptive that is. Children even to a greater extent than adults are very reliant on government services. So education, health care, all of that is disrupted when you have a conflict and when you have children on the move. And we're also seeing, and I think I said this to you all the last board meeting, we're seeing a lot of grave violations against children in conflicts. And I think last year, I'm not sure exactly this year, last year, the most recent report we did was that it's the highest number of grave violations ever reported against children. It's killing, maiming, abducting, sexual violence. I mean, imagine that, right? These are children, for heaven's sake. And this is what we're seeing all around the world. So I think, you know, there's a lot of room here for outrage and for concern about what's happening to children in these settings. I could do one thing, if I had a magic wand, I would stop conflict because I think it is the worst thing for children. And I think, you know, I don't know how to do that. I look to all of you, the political leaders, to try to figure that out. That's not my job. But I mean, it is the impact on children are profound. To the colleague from Panama, I think You mentioned some interesting points about education and food insecurity. And, you know, it got me thinking a little bit, you know, I mean, all of us know children, right? You know, some child probably loves some child in your life. And just imagine that child hungry, not going to school, risk of all sorts of violence. I mean, this is what's happening to children around the world. And sometimes You know, we have so many conversations about it that the numbers and you can forget that these are individual children who are facing just horrible things in the world. And I think that should give all of us a little pause and try to think about how do we protect the most vulnerable. As I said, I would like to stop all conflict. I don't think I have that ability, but we do have to do our best to protect children and make sure the most vulnerable are not suffering the way we know they are. And then finally, to the colleague from Bulgaria, I like you mentioned this, you know, we say this a lot at UNICEF that we stay and deliver. And sometimes that gives me fits because there are places where I would like to try to get people out, UNICEF staff, and they are just, they're stubborn in that way. You know, they want to stay, they want to help, they want to deliver for children, and they are willing to do that at just incredible cost. And they are just the most committed people ever, so huge thank you for acknowledging that.

We see merit in proposals that would increase minimum allocations of core resources to country programs. To conclude, Madam Executive Director, in a context of tensions,

Thank you, Executive Director, and thank you, Mr. President. We value UNICEF's focus on protecting communities through risk communication, infection prevention, essential service continuity, and support for frontline

health workers.

Mr. President, let me express our sincere appreciation to the executive director, Catherine Russell, for her comprehensive opening statement.
